content: 1. Parker SP, Cubitt WD, and Ades AE developed a method to detect and confirm the presence of antibodies to hepatitis C virus (HCV) in dried blood spots. This method was published in the Journal of Virological Methods in 1997. 2. Judd A, Parry J, Hickman M, McDonald T, Jordan L, Lewis K, et al. evaluated a modified commercial assay for detecting HCV antibodies in oral fluids and dried blood spots. Their findings were published in the Journal of Medical Virology in 2003. 3. Parker SP, Khan HI, and Cubitt WD investigated the detection of HCV antibodies in dried blood spot samples collected from mothers and their offspring in Lahore, Pakistan. This study was published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 1999. 4. Greenman J, Roberts T, Cohn J, and Messac L conducted a systematic literature review on the use of dried blood spots for HCV RNA genotyping, quantification, and storage. Their findings were published in the Journal of Viral Hepatitis in 2015. 5. Abe K and Konomi N demonstrated that HCV RNA in dried serum spots on filter paper remains stable at room temperature. This study was published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 1998. 6. Bennett S, Gunson R, McAllister G, Hutchinson SJ, Goldberg DJ, Cameron SO, et al. explored the detection of HCV RNA in dried blood spots. Their research was published in the Journal of Clinical Virology in 2012. 7. De Crignis E, Re MC, Cimatti L, Zecci L, and Gibellini D utilized SYBR Green-based multiplex real-time PCR to detect HIV-1 and HCV in dried blood spots. This study was published in the Journal of Virological Methods in 2010. 8. Santos C, Reis A, Dos Santos CV, Damas C, Silva MH, Viana MV, et al. used real-time PCR to detect HCV RNA in dried blood spots from Brazilian patients with chronic HCV infection. Their findings were published in the Journal of Virological Methods in 2012. 9. Solmone M, Girardi E, Costa F, Pucillo L, Ippolito G, and Capobianchi MR developed a simple and reliable method for detecting and genotyping HCV RNA in dried blood spots stored at room temperature. This study was published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2002. 10. Tuiallion E, Montain A, Meroueh F, Ottomani L, Picot MC, Nagot N, et al. investigated the use of dried blood spots for HCV serology and molecular testing. Their research was published in Hepatology in 2010. 11. Dokubo EK, Evans J, Winkelman V, Cyrus S, Tobler LH, Asher A, et al. compared the detection of HCV RNA and antibodies in dried blood spots versus plasma specimens. This study was published in the Journal of Clinical Virology in 2014. 12. Tejada-Strop A, Drobeniuc J, Mixson-Hayden T, Forbi JC, Le NT, Li L, et al. reported disparate detection outcomes for anti-HCV IgG and HCV RNA in dried blood spots. Their findings were published in the Journal of Virological Methods in 2015. 13. Soulier A, Poiteau L, Rosa I, Hezode C, Roudot-Thoraval F, Pawlotsky JM, et al. highlighted the utility of dried blood spots as a tool to ensure broad access to HCV screening, diagnosis, and treatment monitoring. This study was published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2016. 14. Advances in hepatitis B virus (HBV) detection technology have created new opportunities for improving screening, referral, and treatment. A meta-analysis and review conducted by the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine team assessed the diagnostic accuracy of HBsAg/HBeAg tests compared to nucleic acid testing (NAT) for confirming successful treatment response in HBV patients. 15. The review found that while HBV NAT is considered the gold standard for confirming treatment response, HBsAg and HBeAg tests are valuable for monitoring patients in resource-limited settings where NAT is not readily available. The kinetics of HBsAg and HBV DNA were shown to follow similar profiles during treatment with pegylated interferon (PEG-IFN) and in patients achieving sustained virological response (SVR). 16. Quantification of HBsAg can differentiate active cases of chronic HBV from inactive carriers, reducing the need for rigorous monitoring of HBV DNA levels. HBeAg was found to distinguish late responders from non-responders after 24 weeks of treatment. 17. The systematic review emphasized the need for further studies to determine the utility of HBsAg/HBeAg tests as markers of treatment response for various therapeutic agents. It also highlighted the importance of HBV testing guidelines, particularly in lowand middle-income settings with limited resources. 18. The review included observational studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the sensitivity and specificity of HBsAg/HBeAg tests compared to HBV DNA detection. Only two studies met the inclusion criteria, highlighting the limited evidence available. 19. Larsson et al. (2013) monitored HBsAg levels and HBV DNA quantification in 160 patients treated for chronic HBV infection. The sensitivity of HBsAg compared to HBV DNA was 34%, and specificity was 89%. The study suggested that HBsAg quantification could complement HBV DNA quantification for treatment monitoring. 20. Perrillo et al. (1993) evaluated the HBeAg assay's ability to provide comparable information to HBV DNA assays during and after interferon therapy. The study found that 95% of HBV DNA-positive samples were also positive for HBeAg, but only 56% of HBV DNA-negative patients tested positive for HBeAg. 21. The systematic review concluded that monitoring response to HBV treatment requires both the sustained disappearance of HBV DNA and the clearance of HBsAg/HBeAg from the blood. However, the limited number of studies meeting the inclusion criteria underscores the need for more robust research in this area.
